algorithms-001.question: For an array of n elements, what is the time complexity of comparing every pair of distinct elements exactly once (a double loop that compares element i with every element after it, advancing i one step at a time)?
choices: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
algorithms-001.explanation: The number of pairs compared is (n−1) + (n−2) + … + 1 = n(n−1)/2: 45 for n = 10 and 499,500 for n = 1000. Big-O notation only describes how the count grows as n gets large, so the factor of 1/2 and the lower-order term are dropped, giving O(n²). Doubling n roughly quadruples the count. O(n) is the complexity of looking at each element once, and O(n log n) is that of algorithms such as merge sort that repeatedly split the data in half.
choiceNotes: Looking at each element once would be O(n), but here each element is compared with all of the remaining ones.
This is the complexity of algorithms such as merge sort that repeatedly halve the data, which is smaller than comparing all pairs.
Correct. There are n(n−1)/2 comparisons, which grows in proportion to n².

algorithms-002.question: A program with O(n²) time complexity takes 0.5 seconds for 1,000 data items. About how long will it take for 4,000 items?
choices: 2 seconds
8 seconds
32 seconds
algorithms-002.explanation: With O(n²), the running time is proportional to the square of the data size, so four times the data takes 4² = 16 times as long: 0.5 s × 16 = 8 s. 2 seconds would be the result for O(n), which is proportional to the data size, and 32 seconds for O(n³), which grows with the cube (4³ = 64 times). In practice it can be even slower, for example once the data no longer fits in the cache.
choiceNotes: That would be the case for O(n), which grows in proportion to the data size; with O(n²) the growth is squared.
Correct. Four times the data takes 4² = 16 times as long: 0.5 × 16 = 8 seconds.
This is the value for O(n³), which grows 4³ = 64 times.

algorithms-003.question: A linear search compares the elements of an array of 100 distinct values one by one from the front to find a target. If the target is always in the array and is equally likely to be at any position, what is the average number of comparisons?
choices: About 7
algorithms-003.explanation: If the target is at position k, the search makes k comparisons, so the average is (1 + 2 + … + 100) / 100 = 50.5, or (n + 1)/2 in general. The best case (target at the front) takes 1 comparison and the worst case (target at the end) takes 100; both the average and the worst case are proportional to n, so the complexity is O(n). About 7 corresponds to log₂ 100 ≈ 6.6, the number of steps of a binary search, which cannot be used unless the data is sorted.
choiceNotes: This is close to the maximum for a binary search, not the average for a linear search.
This is the worst case, when the target is at the end.

algorithms-004.question: Compared with an array, which is a correct description of a linked list (a list in which each element holds a pointer to the next element)?
choices: If the element just before the insertion point is known, a new element can be inserted just by changing pointers without moving other elements, but reading the i-th element requires following the list from the front
The position of the i-th element can be computed, so any element can be read in constant time, O(1)
The elements are stored contiguously in memory, so caches and prefetching work well when reading them in order
algorithms-004.explanation: In a linked list, once the position is known, insertion and deletion only require rewriting the neighboring pointers, which takes O(1). Reading the i-th element, however, requires following i pointers from the front, which takes O(n). An array can compute the address of the i-th element from its start address and element size, so it reads any element in O(1), but inserting in the middle takes O(n) to shift the following elements. Also, because array elements are contiguous, caches and prefetching work well, whereas the nodes of a linked list tend to be scattered in memory, so even an O(n) traversal can be much slower.
choiceNotes: Correct. Insertion and deletion are just pointer changes, but reading by position means walking from the front.
Computing the address and reading in O(1) is a property of arrays.
Contiguous storage that suits caches is a property of arrays. Linked list nodes tend to be scattered.

algorithms-005.question: On an empty stack, the operations push 1, push 2, pop, push 3, push 4, pop, pop are performed in this order. In what order are the values removed by pop?
algorithms-005.explanation: A stack is a last-in, first-out (LIFO) structure: the item added last is removed first. After push 1 and push 2, pop removes the top value 2, leaving 1. Pushing 3 and 4 then gives 4, 3, 1 from the top, so the next two pops remove 4 and then 3. The values therefore come out as 2, 4, 3, and 1 remains on the stack. 1, 2, 3 is the order you would get from a queue (first-in, first-out, FIFO), which removes the earliest item first.
choiceNotes: This is the order for a queue (FIFO), which removes items in the order they were added.
4 and 3 are reversed. The 4, pushed later, comes out first.
Correct. The item added last comes out first, giving 2, 4, 3.

algorithms-006.question: Elements A, B and C are added to an empty queue in this order. Then one element is removed, D is added and one is removed, and E is added and one is removed. In what order are the elements removed?
choices: A, B, C
C, D, E
C, B, A
algorithms-006.explanation: A queue is a first-in, first-out (FIFO) structure: items are removed in the order they were added. After A, B and C are added, the first removal takes A. Even though D and E are added at the back afterward, B and C at the front come out first, so the removal order is A, B, C, and D and E remain. C, D, E is the order you would get from a stack (LIFO), which removes the most recently added item each time. Queues are used for print jobs, for message queues that pass data between tasks, and for breadth-first search.
choiceNotes: Correct. B and C, added earlier, come out before D and E.
This is the order for a stack (LIFO), which removes the most recently added item each time.
This is the reverse of the insertion order, not queue order.

algorithms-007.question: The expression “3 4 + 2 * 5 −” in reverse Polish notation (postfix notation) is evaluated by pushing each number onto a stack and, for each operator, popping two values, computing the result and pushing it back. What is the result? The left operand of an operator is the value that was pushed earlier.
algorithms-007.explanation: Push 3 and 4, then + pops them and pushes 3 + 4 = 7. Push 2, then * pushes 7 × 2 = 14. Push 5, then − subtracts the later value 5 from the earlier value 14, giving 14 − 5 = 9. In postfix notation the order of operations is fixed by the sequence itself, so no parentheses are needed; this expression corresponds to (3 + 4) × 2 − 5 in ordinary notation. −9 results from swapping the operands of the subtraction, and 6 from reading it as 3 + 4 × 2 − 5 without parentheses.
choiceNotes: This swaps the operands of the subtraction (5 − 14). The left operand is 14, which was pushed earlier.
This computes 3 + 4 × 2 − 5 without parentheses. In postfix notation the + is done first.

algorithms-008.question: Which is the correct description of a collision in a hash table?
choices: Being able to work out the original key from its hash value
Different keys producing the same hash value (storage position)
The same key producing a different hash value each time the program runs
algorithms-008.explanation: A hash table computes a storage position from the key with a hash function, allowing search, insertion and deletion in O(1) on average. Because there are far more possible keys than table slots, different keys landing on the same position (a collision) cannot be avoided. Collisions are therefore handled by methods such as chaining, which links the elements at the same position into a list, or open addressing, which looks for another free position. The same key must always produce the same hash value or lookups would fail, and whether the key can be recovered from the hash value is a property that matters for cryptographic use, not collisions.
choiceNotes: Not being able to recover the input (one-wayness) is a property of cryptographic hash functions, which is a separate matter from collisions.
Correct. Different keys mapping to the same position is a collision, and it must always be handled somehow.
If the same key gave different values, data could not be found, so hash functions are designed not to do this.

algorithms-009.question: Keys 10, 17, 24 and 3 are stored in this order in a hash table of size 7 (positions 0 to 6) with the hash function h(k) = k mod 7. Collisions are resolved by linear probing, which moves forward one position at a time (wrapping from 6 to 0) to find a free slot. At which position is key 3 stored?
choices: Position 3
Position 4
Position 6
algorithms-009.explanation: All four keys leave a remainder of 3 when divided by 7, so each one first tries position 3. Key 10 goes into position 3; 17 finds position 3 taken and goes into position 4; 24 finds positions 3 and 4 taken and goes into position 5. Key 3 finds positions 3, 4 and 5 taken and is stored at position 6. As this shows, linear probing makes occupied positions bunch together (clustering), so keys that arrive later need more probes.
choiceNotes: This is the hash value itself, but 10 is already there.
This is where 17 went. Position 5 after it is also taken by 24.
Correct. Positions 3, 4 and 5 are taken, so it goes into the free position 6.

algorithms-010.question: Which correctly compares chaining (linking the elements at the same position into a linked list) and open addressing (finding another free position within the table) as ways to resolve hash table collisions? The load factor is the number of stored elements divided by the table size.
choices: Chaining can store elements even when the load factor exceeds 1, but open addressing cannot store more elements than the table size, and its number of probes rises sharply as the load factor approaches 1
Open addressing has no collisions, so a search always takes one probe regardless of the load factor
With chaining, the search cost stays the same however high the load factor becomes
algorithms-010.explanation: Chaining links elements at the same position into lists, so it can store more elements than the table size, but the average list length grows in proportion to the load factor and so does the search cost. Open addressing stores everything inside the table, so it can hold at most as many elements as the table size, and the number of probes to find a free slot rises sharply as the load factor approaches 1. With either method, it is usual to enlarge the table and reinsert all elements (rehash) once the load factor exceeds a chosen limit, such as about 0.5 to 0.75. Collisions also occur in open addressing; it handles them by looking for a free position.
choiceNotes: Correct. It accurately describes the difference in capacity and in how searches slow down at high load factors.
Collisions also occur in open addressing; it handles them by looking for another free position.
The average list length is proportional to the load factor, so a high load factor makes searches slower.

algorithms-011.question: Which is a prerequisite for using binary search, which compares the target with the middle element and halves the search range each time?
choices: The number of data items must be a power of two
The data must be sorted by key
The data must not contain duplicate values
algorithms-011.explanation: Binary search uses the result of comparing the target with the middle element to decide whether the target lies in the first or second half, and halves the range. That conclusion holds only because the data is sorted, so binary search cannot be used on an unsorted array. The number of items does not need to be a power of two; choosing the middle as (low + high) ÷ 2 rounded down works for any size. Duplicates are also fine: one of the matching values is found (finding the first occurrence takes a small extra step).
choiceNotes: Choosing the middle by rounding down works for any number of items.
Correct. Because the data is sorted, a comparison with the middle element tells you which half to keep.
Search still works with duplicates; one of the matching values is found.

algorithms-012.question: A binary search is performed on 1,000 distinct values sorted in ascending order. If one comparison tells you whether the values are equal, smaller or larger, what is the maximum number of comparisons, counting both successful and unsuccessful searches?
algorithms-012.explanation: Each comparison roughly halves the search range, and 2¹⁰ = 1024 ≥ 1000, so the range is used up after at most 10 comparisons (⌊log₂ 1000⌋ + 1 = 10). The complexity is O(log n), and even 1,000,000 values need at most 20 comparisons. 32 corresponds to √1000 ≈ 31.6, and 500 is close to the average for a linear search (about n/2). Keep in mind, though, that binary search needs sorted data, and sorting itself costs O(n log n).
choiceNotes: Correct. 2¹⁰ = 1024 ≥ 1000, so at most 10 comparisons are needed.
This corresponds to √1000 and has nothing to do with binary search.
This is close to the average number of comparisons for a linear search.

algorithms-013.question: A binary search looks for 38 in the ascending array a[0] to a[9] = 3, 8, 12, 17, 23, 31, 38, 45, 52, 60. The search range starts with lo = 0 and hi = 9, and the middle position is (lo + hi) ÷ 2 rounded down. Which lists, in order, the elements compared with 38?
algorithms-013.explanation: First, (0 + 9) ÷ 2 = 4, so 38 is compared with a[4] = 23; 38 is larger, so lo = 5. Next, (5 + 9) ÷ 2 = 7, so it is compared with a[7] = 45; 38 is smaller, so hi = 6. Then (5 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5 gives a[5] = 31, so lo = 6, and finally a[6] = 38 matches. That is 4 comparisons, the maximum for 10 elements, ⌊log₂ 10⌋ + 1 = 4. The order 31, 52, 45, 38 results from rounding the middle up, which is not the rule given in the question.
choiceNotes: After comparing with 23, the next comparison is with a[7] = 45, the middle of the remaining range a[5] to a[9].
This is the order when the middle is rounded up, which differs from the rule in the question.
Correct. It compares a[4], a[7], a[5] and a[6] in turn and finds the value on the fourth comparison.

algorithms-014.question: The array 5, 3, 8, 1, 4 is sorted in ascending order with bubble sort. What is the array after one pass, in which neighboring elements are compared from the front to the end and swapped whenever the left one is larger?
algorithms-014.explanation: Swapping 5 and 3 gives 3, 5, 8, 1, 4; 5 and 8 stay; swapping 8 and 1 gives 3, 5, 1, 8, 4; and swapping 8 and 4 gives 3, 5, 1, 4, 8. One pass carries the maximum value 8 all the way to the end, fixing its position, and the next pass sorts the remaining four elements in the same way. 1, 3, 8, 5, 4 is the array after one pass of selection sort, which swaps the minimum to the front, and 1, 3, 4, 5, 8 is the fully sorted result.
choiceNotes: This is the array after one pass of selection sort, which swaps the minimum value 1 to the front.
Correct. Swapping neighbors carries the maximum value 8 to the end.
This is the final sorted result; one pass does not get this far.

algorithms-015.question: The array 29, 10, 14, 37, 13 is sorted in ascending order with selection sort, which finds the minimum of the unsorted part and swaps it with the first element of the unsorted part. What is the array after this step has been done twice?
algorithms-015.explanation: The first step swaps the overall minimum 10 with 29 at the front, giving 10, 29, 14, 37, 13. The second step swaps 13, the minimum from the second element on, with 29 in the second position, giving 10, 13, 14, 37, 29. Selection sort always makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons but at most one swap per step, which can be an advantage when writes are expensive. 10, 14, 29, 37, 13 is the array after insertion sort has inserted two elements, and 10, 14, 13, 29, 37 is the array after two passes of bubble sort.
choiceNotes: Correct. 10 and then 13 are swapped to the front.
This is the array after insertion sort has inserted 10 and 14.
This is the array after two passes of bubble sort.

algorithms-016.question: An array of 10 elements is sorted in ascending order with insertion sort. Each element from the second one on is taken out and compared with the elements to its left, starting with its left neighbor, until an element less than or equal to it is found or the front is reached. How many comparisons are made when the array is already in ascending order, and when it is in descending order?
choices: 45 in both cases
9 and 45
algorithms-016.explanation: If the array is already ascending, each element needs only one comparison with its left neighbor, so the 9 elements take 9 comparisons in total. If it is descending, the element taken out i-th is compared with all i elements to its left, giving 1 + 2 + … + 9 = 45. Insertion sort thus varies greatly with the input, O(n) in the best case and O(n²) in the worst, and it is very fast on nearly sorted data. Shell sort exploits this by first running insertion sort on elements a gap apart, and Timsort also uses insertion sort for short runs.
choiceNotes: Always making 45 comparisons is true of selection sort. For insertion sort the count depends on the input order.
The element count 10 and 10² = 100 are not the comparison counts.
Correct. Ascending order takes one comparison per element (9), and descending order takes 1 + 2 + … + 9 = 45.

algorithms-017.question: Which sorting algorithm is O(n log n) even in the worst case and sorts with almost no extra memory such as a work array?
choices: Merge sort
Heapsort
Quicksort
algorithms-017.explanation: Heapsort builds a binary heap inside the array and repeatedly swaps the maximum at the root with the last element and shrinks the heap, so it runs in O(n log n) even in the worst case and needs only a constant amount of extra memory. Merge sort is also O(n log n) in the worst case, but on an array it needs a work area proportional to n. Quicksort is O(n log n) on average and fast in practice, but depending on the pivot choice and the data it can degrade to O(n²). Note that heapsort compares elements that are far apart, so its cache efficiency is poor, and it is not stable.
choiceNotes: It is O(n log n) in the worst case, but on an array it needs a work area proportional to n.
Correct. It is O(n log n) even in the worst case and sorts within the array itself.
It is O(n log n) on average but O(n²) in the worst case.

algorithms-018.question: The (name, score) records (A, 80), (B, 70), (C, 80), (D, 70) are in this order. If they are sorted by score in ascending order with a stable sort, in what order do the names appear?
choices: B, D, A, C
D, B, A, C
B, D, C, A
algorithms-018.explanation: A stable sort keeps elements with the same key (here, the score) in their original relative order. B and D, both with 70, stay in the order B, D, and A and C, both with 80, stay in the order A, C, giving B, D, A, C. Bubble sort, insertion sort and merge sort are stable, while selection sort, quicksort and heapsort are generally not. With a stable sort you can sort by several keys, for example sorting by name first and then by score.
choiceNotes: Correct. Records with the same score keep their original order (B before D, A before C).
B and D, both with 70, are in the reverse of their original order.
A and C, both with 80, are in the reverse of their original order.

algorithms-019.question: Which is a typical case in which quicksort takes O(n²) time?
choices: The data is in random order and the pivot is chosen at random
The number of data items is a power of two
The data is already sorted and the first element is always used as the pivot
algorithms-019.explanation: Quicksort splits the elements into those smaller and those larger than the pivot, then splits each part again. If the data is already sorted and the first element is always the pivot, the pivot is the minimum every time and each split is lopsided, with zero elements on one side and all the rest on the other, so it makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons (4,950 for n = 100). Choosing the pivot at random or as the median of three values makes a long run of lopsided splits extremely unlikely. The number of items has nothing to do with this.
choiceNotes: With a random pivot, lopsided splits are extremely unlikely to keep happening, and it averages O(n log n).
Whether the count is a power of two has nothing to do with lopsided splits.
Correct. The pivot is the minimum every time, so the splits are extremely lopsided.

algorithms-020.question: In merge sort, the two sorted runs 1, 4, 7, 9 and 2, 3, 8, 10 are merged into one by repeatedly comparing their front elements and outputting the smaller. When one run is empty, the rest of the other is output without comparisons. How many comparisons are made?
algorithms-020.explanation: The comparisons are 1 vs 2, 4 vs 2, 4 vs 3, 4 vs 8, 7 vs 8, 9 vs 8 and 9 vs 10; at that point the first run is empty, so the remaining 10 is output without a comparison. That is 7 comparisons, the maximum m + n − 1 = 7 for merging runs of lengths m and n. A merge looks at each element of the sorted runs only once, so it takes O(m + n), and since merge sort repeats this over log₂ n levels, the whole sort takes O(n log n).
choiceNotes: It is not enough to compare only as many times as one run's length. The values alternate between the runs, so more comparisons are needed.
Correct. Only the last value, 10, is output without a comparison, so there are 7 comparisons.
The last element has nothing left to be compared with, so the count is not 8.

algorithms-021.question: A binary heap is stored in an array a[0], a[1], a[2], … with the root at a[0], filling each level from left to right starting at the top. Which are the children and the parent of a[4]?
choices: Children a[9] and a[10]; parent a[1]
Children a[8] and a[9]; parent a[2]
Children a[9] and a[10]; parent a[2]
algorithms-021.explanation: With the root at a[0], the children of a[i] are a[2i+1] and a[2i+2], and its parent is a[(i−1) ÷ 2, rounded down]. For i = 4, the children are a[9] and a[10] and the parent is a[(4−1) ÷ 2] = a[1]. With the root at a[1], the children are a[2i] and a[2i+1] and the parent is a[i ÷ 2], so it is important to check which convention is being used. Because a heap is a complete binary tree, it can be stored in an array without pointers, and parents and children are found by index arithmetic alone.
choiceNotes: Correct. The children are 2×4+1 = 9 and 2×4+2 = 10, and the parent is (4−1) ÷ 2 = 1.
This applies the formulas for a root at a[1] (children 2i and 2i+1, parent i ÷ 2).
The children are right, but the parent is (4−1) ÷ 2 rounded down, which is a[1].

algorithms-022.question: A max-heap, in which each parent's value is at least as large as its children's, is stored in an array with the root at a[0]. 45 is added to the heap 50, 30, 40, 10, 20, 35 by placing it at the end and then swapping it with its parent as long as it is larger than the parent. What is the resulting array?
algorithms-022.explanation: 45 is placed at a[6], whose parent is a[(6−1) ÷ 2] = a[2] = 40. Since 45 > 40, they are swapped and 45 moves to a[2]. Its next parent, a[0] = 50, is larger than 45, so the process stops, giving 50, 30, 45, 10, 20, 35, 40. Swaps happen at most as many times as the height of the tree, so insertion takes O(log n), and removing the maximum is also O(log n). For this reason, binary heaps are commonly used to implement priority queues.
choiceNotes: It has only been placed at the end; it was not swapped even though it is larger than its parent 40.
This moves 45 all the way to the root, although it is smaller than the root 50.
Correct. After swapping with 40, it stops because its parent 50 is larger.

algorithms-023.question: When a binary search tree is traversed in in-order (visiting the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree), how are the values of the visited nodes ordered? Assume all values are distinct.
choices: In ascending order (smallest first)
In the order they were inserted
In order of closeness to the root (shallowest first)
algorithms-023.explanation: In a binary search tree, for every node, all values in the left subtree are smaller than the node and all values in the right subtree are larger. Visiting the left subtree, the node and then the right subtree therefore visits the values from smallest to largest, so the result is in ascending order. Visiting nodes in order of closeness to the root is a breadth-first (level-order) traversal, which goes level by level from left to right. The insertion order affects the shape of the tree but does not match the order of any of these traversals.
choiceNotes: Correct. Since the left side is smaller and the right side larger, in-order traversal gives ascending order.
The insertion order affects the tree's shape, but in-order traversal gives ascending order regardless of it.
This is the result of a breadth-first (level-order) traversal, which visits the tree level by level.

algorithms-024.question: The values 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 are inserted in this order into an empty binary search tree. In what order are the nodes visited when the tree is traversed in post-order (left subtree, right subtree, then the node)?
algorithms-024.explanation: The root is 50; its left child is 30 (with children 20 and 40) and its right child is 70 (with children 60 and 80). Post-order visits the left subtree as 20, 40, 30 and the right subtree as 60, 80, 70, and only then the root 50. 50, 30, 20, 40, 70, 60, 80 is the pre-order result, which visits each node first, and 20, 30, 40, … is the in-order result. Post-order is used when children must be processed first, such as when deleting a tree or producing postfix notation from an expression tree.
choiceNotes: This is the pre-order result, which visits each node before its subtrees.
Correct. Each node is visited after its left and right subtrees, so the root 50 comes last.
This is the in-order result, which lists the values in ascending order.

algorithms-025.question: The values 1, 2, 3, …, 1000 are inserted in this order into an empty binary search tree (no rebalancing is done). When searching this tree for 1000, how many nodes are compared, starting from the root, before it is found?
algorithms-025.explanation: When values are inserted in ascending order, each new value becomes the right child of the previous maximum, so the tree becomes a single chain extending only to the right (height 999). 1000 is at the very bottom, so it is compared with all 1,000 nodes, 1, 2, …, 1000, which is O(n), the same as walking a linked list from the front. A balanced tree would have only about log₂ 1000 ≈ 10 levels, so using a self-balancing binary search tree such as an AVL tree or a red-black tree, which reshapes itself on every insertion and deletion, keeps the worst case at O(log n).
choiceNotes: A balanced tree would need about 10, but this tree has become a single chain.
This is close to searching for a value in the middle, but 1000 is at the end.
Correct. The tree is a single chain, so finding 1000 means comparing every node.

algorithms-026.question: What is the main reason that B-trees (including B+ trees), rather than binary search trees, are widely used for indexes in databases and file systems?
choices: Each node holds many keys, which keeps the tree shallow and narrows the range greatly with each node read, reducing the number of block reads from disk or similar storage
Each node holds only one key, so fewer comparisons are needed than in a binary search tree
The tree does not need to be reshaped on insertion, so it is simpler to implement than a binary search tree
algorithms-026.explanation: Disks and SSDs read data in blocks of several kilobytes even when only one byte is needed, so reducing the number of reads matters. A B-tree puts hundreds of keys into one node (one block), so each node read branches hundreds of ways; even 100 million records can be reached in 3 to 4 levels. When an insertion or deletion overfills a node it is split, and when a node becomes too empty it is merged, keeping all leaves at the same depth. A binary search tree with 100 million records needs at least about 27 levels, and reading a different block at each level is slow.
choiceNotes: Correct. A high branching factor keeps the tree shallow and reduces the number of block reads.
Holding many keys per node is what characterizes a B-tree.
B-trees also reshape themselves by splitting and merging nodes, keeping all leaves at the same depth.

algorithms-027.question: Which is an appropriate way to store in memory a sparse graph, one with few edges compared with its number of vertices, such as a road network with about 1 million vertices and 3 million edges?
choices: An adjacency matrix: it can check whether two vertices are connected in O(1) and also uses the least memory
Adjacency lists: memory is proportional to the number of vertices plus the number of edges, and they suit following the edges out of a vertex one by one
An adjacency matrix: its memory is proportional only to the number of edges
algorithms-027.explanation: An adjacency matrix uses a V × V table for V vertices, so 1 million vertices need 10¹² entries, about 125 GB even at 1 bit per entry. Adjacency lists store only the neighbors of each vertex, so memory is O(V + E), only a few million entries in this example. An adjacency matrix has the advantage of checking for an edge in O(1) and suits dense graphs or graphs with few vertices. For processing that follows the edges out of each vertex in turn, such as breadth-first search and Dijkstra's algorithm, adjacency lists are more efficient.
choiceNotes: Checking for an edge in O(1) is true, but the memory grows with the square of the number of vertices, which is very wasteful for a sparse graph.
Correct. Memory is only O(V + E), and they suit processing that walks through neighboring vertices.
The size of an adjacency matrix does not depend on the number of edges; it is the square of the number of vertices.

algorithms-028.question: In a graph whose edges have no weights, you want to find the smallest number of edges from a starting vertex to every other vertex. Which pair of search method and data structure is suitable?
choices: Breadth-first search with a queue
Depth-first search with a stack
Breadth-first search with a stack
algorithms-028.explanation: Breadth-first search visits vertices in order of distance: first those one edge from the start, then those two edges away, and so on. Adding each newly found vertex to the back of a queue and taking vertices from the front preserves this nearest-first order, so the number of edges when a vertex is first reached is the shortest. Depth-first search (using recursion or a stack) goes as far as it can along one path, so it may first reach a vertex by a roundabout route, and shortest distances are not guaranteed. Using a stack instead of a queue turns the traversal into something close to depth-first search.
choiceNotes: Correct. A queue makes the search visit vertices nearest-first, which gives the smallest number of edges.
Depth-first search can first reach a vertex by a roundabout route, so it does not guarantee shortest distances.
With a stack, the most recently found vertex is examined first, so vertices are no longer visited nearest-first.

algorithms-029.question: In an undirected graph, the neighbors of each vertex are A: B, C / B: A, D, E / C: A, F / D: B / E: B, F / F: C, E. A recursive depth-first search starts from vertex A. The neighbors are examined in the order listed, and as soon as an unvisited vertex is found, the search moves to it. In what order are the vertices visited?
choices: A, B, C, D, E, F
A, B, D, E, C, F
A, B, D, E, F, C
algorithms-029.explanation: From A the search moves to B, then to D, the first unvisited neighbor of B. D's only neighbor, B, is already visited, so it returns to B and moves on to E, then from E to the unvisited F, and from F to its neighbor C. The order is therefore A, B, D, E, F, C. A, B, C, D, E, F is the breadth-first search order, which visits vertices nearest-first. A, B, D, E, C, F turns back from E without going to the unvisited F, so it is not a depth-first order.
choiceNotes: This is the breadth-first search order, which visits vertices nearest-first.
E has an unvisited neighbor F, so the search goes to F before returning toward C.
Correct. The search goes as far as it can and backtracks only at dead ends.

algorithms-030.question: In an undirected graph, the edge weights (distances) are S−A: 4, S−B: 1, A−B: 2, A−C: 1, B−C: 5, C−T: 3 and A−T: 6. Which shows the shortest path from S to T found by Dijkstra's algorithm and its length?
choices: S→A→C→T, length 8
S→B→A→C→T, length 7
S→B→C→T, length 9
algorithms-030.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly finalizes the nearest vertex whose distance is not yet final and updates the distances of its neighbors. From S (0), B is finalized at 1, and going through B gives A a distance of 1 + 2 = 3, shorter than the direct 4. Finalizing A (3) gives C 3 + 1 = 4 and T 3 + 6 = 9, and finalizing C (4) updates T to 4 + 3 = 7. The shortest path is therefore S→B→A→C→T with length 7. S→A→C→T (8) is longer because it takes S−A directly, and S→B→C→T (9) is longer because B−C has the large weight 5.
choiceNotes: Going from S to A through B (1 + 2 = 3) is shorter than going directly (4).
Correct. S→B (1), B→A (2), A→C (1) and C→T (3) total 7.
B−C has a large weight of 5, so going through A is shorter.

algorithms-031.question: Which condition on the graph is required for Dijkstra's algorithm to find correct shortest paths?
choices: The graph has no cycles (paths that return to the same vertex)
The edges have no direction
All edge weights are 0 or greater
algorithms-031.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm finalizes the unfinalized vertex with the smallest distance. This relies on the assumption that going through other vertices can only increase a distance, never decrease it. With a negative edge, a distance can become shorter later through another route; for example, in a directed graph with S→A 2, S→B 3 and B→A −2, A is finalized at 2 before the path S→B→A of length 1 is found. When negative weights exist, the Bellman-Ford algorithm or similar methods are used. Dijkstra's algorithm works with cycles and with directed edges as long as all weights are 0 or greater.
choiceNotes: It works correctly with cycles as long as the weights are 0 or greater; road networks are full of cycles.
It also works on directed graphs.
Correct. With negative weights, a finalized distance can later turn out to be shorter.

algorithms-032.question: Tasks A to E have the ordering constraints “A before C”, “B before C”, “C before D”, “B before E” and “E before D”. Which order satisfies all the constraints (a result of topological sorting)?
choices: A, C, B, E, D
B, A, E, C, D
B, E, D, A, C
algorithms-032.explanation: In B, A, E, C, D, A and B come before C, C and E come before D, and B comes before E, so all five constraints are met. A, C, B, E, D does C before B, violating “B before C”, and B, E, D, A, C does D before C, violating “C before D”. Topological sorting arranges the vertices of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) so that every edge points from earlier to later; it can be done by repeatedly taking a vertex with no incoming edges (Kahn's algorithm) or with depth-first search. The answer is not always unique: this example has five valid orders.
choiceNotes: It does C before B, violating “B before C”.
Correct. It satisfies all five constraints.
It does D before C, violating “C before D”.

algorithms-033.question: A function f(x, y) is defined as “if y is 0, return x; otherwise return f(y, x mod y)”. When f(84, 36) is called, what is the return value, and how many times is f called, including the first call?
choices: Returns 12; called 3 times
Returns 12; called 4 times
Returns 6; called 3 times
algorithms-033.explanation: f(84, 36) calls f(36, 12) because 84 mod 36 = 12; that calls f(12, 0) because 36 mod 12 = 0; and since y is 0, it returns 12. The calls are f(84, 36), f(36, 12) and f(12, 0), three in total, and this is the Euclidean algorithm for the greatest common divisor. Because the function returns the result of its recursive call directly (tail recursion), a compiler that performs tail call optimization can turn it into a loop, so it does not keep using stack space however deep the recursion goes.
choiceNotes: Correct. f(84, 36) → f(36, 12) → f(12, 0), three calls, returning 12, the greatest common divisor of 84 and 36.
The recursion ends at f(12, 0), when y becomes 0, so there is no fourth call.
The greatest common divisor of 84 and 36 is 12 (84 = 12 × 7, 36 = 12 × 3).

algorithms-034.question: A function fib(n) for Fibonacci numbers is defined recursively as “if n is 1 or less, return n; otherwise return fib(n−1) + fib(n−2)”. When fib(5) is called, how many times is fib called, including the first call?
algorithms-034.explanation: Let C(n) be the number of calls for fib(n). Then C(0) = C(1) = 1 and C(n) = 1 + C(n−1) + C(n−2), so C(2) = 3, C(3) = 5, C(4) = 9 and C(5) = 15. Because the same values are recomputed again and again, the count grows exponentially with n; fib(30) makes about 2.69 million calls. With memoization (a form of dynamic programming), which stores computed values in a table, only the six values fib(0) to fib(5) are computed and the calls drop to 9 (2n − 1). 6 is the number of distinct arguments, and 9 is the number of calls with memoization.
choiceNotes: This is the number of distinct arguments fib(0) to fib(5); it does not count recomputation of the same values.
This is the number of calls with memoization, where a value already computed is returned from a table.
Correct. From C(n) = 1 + C(n−1) + C(n−2), C(5) = 15.

algorithms-035.question: You pay 8 yen with coins of 1 yen, 4 yen and 6 yen. Which correctly relates the number of coins chosen by a greedy algorithm, which uses as many of the largest coin as possible first, to the minimum number of coins?
choices: The greedy algorithm also reaches the minimum of 2 coins
The greedy algorithm uses 3 coins and misses the minimum of 2
The greedy algorithm uses 3 coins, and that is the minimum
algorithms-035.explanation: The greedy algorithm first takes one 6-yen coin and pays the remaining 2 yen with two 1-yen coins, for 3 coins. But two 4-yen coins pay it with just 2. Because a greedy algorithm only accumulates the choice that looks best at each moment, it is not optimal for some coin systems. Dynamic programming, which fills in a table of the minimum number of coins for every amount from 0 to 8 yen in increasing order, always finds the minimum. For coin systems such as Japan's 1, 5, 10, 50, 100 and 500 yen, the greedy algorithm always gives the minimum.
choiceNotes: The greedy algorithm picks the 6-yen coin first, so it never reaches the two-4-yen combination.
Correct. Greedy gives 6 + 1 + 1, three coins; the minimum is 4 + 4, two coins.
Two 4-yen coins pay it with 2 coins, so 3 is not the minimum.

algorithms-036.question: A knapsack with capacity 8 is filled with items chosen from four items with (weight, value) of (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 5) and (5, 6). There is only one of each item and items cannot be split. What is the maximum total value with a total weight of 8 or less?
algorithms-036.explanation: Choosing the items of weight 3 and 5 gives weight 8 and value 4 + 6 = 10, which is the maximum. Weights 2 and 5 (value 9) or 3 and 4 (value 9) also fit but fall short of 10, and any three items weigh at least 2 + 3 + 4 = 9, over the capacity. A greedy algorithm that packs items in order of value per unit weight takes the items of weight 2 and 3 (value 7), and then no item fits in the remaining capacity of 3, so it stops at 7. Dynamic programming updates a table of the best value achievable within each capacity c item by item, and finds the optimum in O(nW) for n items and capacity W.
choiceNotes: This is the result of a greedy algorithm that packs by value per unit weight, which is not optimal.
This is the value of weights 2 and 5, or 3 and 4, which is not the maximum.
Correct. The items of weight 3 and 5 use the capacity of 8 exactly and give a value of 10.

algorithms-037.question: Which is a characteristic of the Boyer-Moore algorithm for finding a pattern in a string?
choices: It compares the pattern starting from its last character and uses information such as the mismatched text character not appearing in the pattern to shift the pattern a long way at once
It shifts the pattern one character at a time from the start of the text and compares every character of the pattern from first to last each time
It sorts both the text and the pattern and then finds the pattern by binary search
algorithms-037.explanation: The Boyer-Moore algorithm compares the pattern from its last character and precomputes tables so that, for example, if the mismatched text character does not appear in the pattern at all, the whole pattern can be shifted past it. As a result, on natural-language text it can skip many characters without comparing them. With a text of length n and a pattern of length m, the naive method that shifts one character at a time and compares everything takes O(nm) in the worst case. The KMP algorithm also uses mismatch information to shift, but it compares from the start of the pattern and guarantees O(n + m) even in the worst case.
choiceNotes: Correct. Comparing from the end and making large shifts based on the mismatched character is the Boyer-Moore algorithm.
This is the naive (brute-force) method, which takes O(nm) in the worst case.
The task is to find positions within the string, and sorting would destroy the position information.

algorithms-038.question: A dynamic array, when an element is added while it is full, allocates a new area with twice the capacity and copies all elements into it. If 1,000 elements are added one at a time to an empty array of capacity 1, how many element copies are made in total?
algorithms-038.explanation: The capacity doubles each time it fills up, going 1, 2, 4, …, 512, and each time all current elements are copied, so the total number of copies is 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 512 = 1,023. For 1,000 additions that is about one copy per element, so the cost per addition is constant on average: amortized O(1). If the capacity grew by only 1 each time, the copies would total 1 + 2 + … + 999 = 499,500, which is O(n²). 10 is the number of reallocations, not the number of elements copied.
choiceNotes: This is the number of reallocations (10, from 1→2 up to 512→1024), not the number of elements copied.
Correct. 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 512 = 1,023, about one copy per addition on average.
This is the total number of copies if the capacity grew by 1 each time.

algorithms-039.question: For a hash table with many elements kept at a load factor of about 0.5, which is the most appropriate reason that open addressing with linear probing tends to be faster than chaining (linking elements with linked lists)?
choices: After a collision, the next position checked is the neighboring element, which is often in the same cache line or the next one, so fewer memory accesses are needed
Open addressing has no collisions at all
Chaining must compute the hash function two or more times
algorithms-039.explanation: On modern CPUs, reading main memory after a cache miss takes far longer than computations such as comparisons. Linear probing checks the neighboring position after a collision, so most probes stay within the same cache line, and prefetching also helps. With chaining, the next element of a list is often somewhere else in memory, so each pointer followed is likely to cause a cache miss. Even with the same big-O complexity, the real speed can differ greatly depending on how memory is accessed. However, linear probing slows down sharply at high load factors as occupied positions cluster, so the load factor is kept fairly low.
choiceNotes: Correct. It only checks neighboring positions, so the data needed is likely to be in the cache already.
Collisions also occur in open addressing; it handles them by checking the neighboring positions.
Both compute the hash function once; the difference is in how memory is accessed.

algorithms-040.question: Sorting methods with a fixed sequence of compare-exchange steps (sorting networks), such as bitonic sort, are sometimes used for sorting on parallel hardware such as GPUs. Why?
choices: They make O(n) comparisons, fewer than the O(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorting
They are stable sorts that keep elements with equal keys in their original order
Which pairs of elements are compared and swapped is fixed in advance regardless of the data values, so many threads can work in the same steps at the same time with uniform branching
algorithms-040.explanation: In bitonic sort, the pairs compared at each stage are determined by their indices alone, and all compare-exchange operations within a stage can run at the same time. n = 2ᵏ items are sorted in k(k+1)/2 stages: 16 items take 10 stages and 80 comparisons in total, and 1,024 items take 55 stages and 28,160 comparisons. The total number of comparisons is O(n log² n), more than quicksort and similar algorithms, but because the steps do not depend on the data, devices like GPUs, where many threads execute the same instructions, run them efficiently without divergent branches. No method that sorts by comparisons alone can use fewer than O(n log n) comparisons, and bitonic sort is generally not stable either.
choiceNotes: No comparison sort can do better than O(n log n) comparisons; bitonic sort makes O(n log² n) comparisons in total.
Bitonic sort also swaps elements that are far apart, so it is generally not stable.
Correct. Because the steps do not depend on the data, many threads can process them simultaneously with uniform branching.
